record.original_question: Can all positive integers be covered by n geometric progressions of integers?

evidence.quote: Is it possible to cover all (positive) integers with n geometrical progressions of integers? Comment: (a) No.

artifact.self_contained_problem: A geometric progression of integers is a set of the form $\{a r^k : k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\}$, where $a$ and $r$ are integers with $|r| \geq 2$ and $a \neq 0$. Determine whether there exists a positive integer $n$ and geometric progressions of integers $G_1, G_2, \dots, G_n$ such that every positive integer belongs to at least one of $G_1, \dots, G_n$. Equivalently, can the set of positive integers be written as the union of finitely many integer geometric progressions?
artifact.status_search_result: The answer is negative and follows from a simple counting/density argument: a single geometric progression $\{a r^k\}$ with $|r|\geq 2$ contains at most $O(\log N)$ elements up to $N$, so any finite union contains $O(\log N)$ integers up to $N$, which cannot cover all $N$ positive integers up to $N$ for large $N$. This is a well-known elementary observation.

status_evidence.title: Geometric progression density
status_evidence.snippet: A geometric progression a, ar, ar^2,... grows exponentially, so it contains only O(log N) terms up to N.
status_evidence.claim: Finite unions of integer geometric progressions have logarithmic counting function and so cannot cover all positive integers.
